catalog_quote: A possible explanation for this may be language contact with Nyasang. The iambic rhythm of Bangru places stress on the second syllable and reduces the initial syllable, but the trochaic rhythm of Nyasang stresses the initial syllable and reduces the final syllable. ... The Bangru word, in particular the Bangru verb, can consist of several prefixes, suffixes and perhaps infixes, whose description would go beyond the scope of this paper. Unstressed, phonologically reduced syllables of the form V or CiV are commonly aligned to the left of the fully formed stressed syllables of the form Ci(G)V(Cf). The reduced syllables contain reduced vowels, i.e. a pre-glottalised back vowel /a/ or an epenthetic schwa /ə/. In the majority of cases, these are prefixes, which Bangru has largely preserved.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bangru words are sesquisyllabic: a reduced, unstressed prefix syllable (V or CəV with schwa or pre-glottalised /a/) precedes the full, stressed root syllable Ci(G)V(Cf). Stress therefore falls on the full root syllable, which in the canonical prefix+root word is the second syllable; the authors describe this as iambic rhythm (in contrast to trochaic Nyasang/Nyishi). The paper treats the short-falling-pitch/glottalised vs long-level-pitch root contrast as open vs closed syllable, not as tone or vowel length, so Bangru is analysed as non-tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. The paper notes that some speakers add an epenthetic breathy final syllable [i̤] to words ending in the affricate (məpot͡ɕ ~ məpot͡ɕi̤ 'shoulder'), which it attributes to contact with trochaic Nyasang; the stress remark is made in that context rather than in a dedicated stress section.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefix + root structure); the remark is brief and in passing, and the paper explicitly says a full description of Bangru word structure (prefixes, suffixes, infixes) is beyond its scope. Reading 'morphologically determined' chosen over the literal 'fixed: second syllable' because the unstressed syllable is defined as the reduced prefix and the stressed syllable as the fully formed root; the field wordlist (Zenodo 1116263) shows some transcribers marking initial stress with an apostrophe (e.g. 'bɛləgəː, 'məriː [C]), which the published analysis does not endorse.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Sarli-circle (India) variety recorded from seven informants in December 2013; it is the only variety Glottolog bang1369 covers. A second variety spoken in Longzi County, Tibet ('China dialect', Bengru 崩如) is described only in Li Daqin 2003 (Chinese), whose forms carry tone letters (⁵⁵, ³¹, ⁵³) in Bodt & Lieberherr's comparison file, so that description may treat the Tibet variety as tonal; it was not accessible.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 (ms p. 6): 'The iambic rhythm of Bangru places stress on the second syllable and reduces the initial syllable' (vs trochaic Nyasang). Sec. 3.4 (ms p. 11): unstressed reduced prefix syllables V/CiV with /a/ or schwa are aligned left of the fully formed stressed syllable Ci(G)V(Cf). Sec. 3.3: short vowel + falling pitch + glottalisation vs long vowel + level pitch analysed as closed vs open syllable, 'rather than a difference in tone or vowel length'.

sources.note: No rule; some transcribers mark stress with an apostrophe on individual forms (e.g. 'bɛləgəː 'borrow', 'məriː [C] 'bone', 'mɛdzo [B] 'burn'), mostly word-initial; the only prose note on stress ('the prefix is stressed') concerns a Koro comparandum.

sources.citation: Bodt, T.A. & I. Lieberherr. 2017. Pitch, vowel length and phonation type in Bangru: a case study (PRAAT acoustic analysis). In: Bangru Language Data, Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.1116263
sources.note: No word-stress statement. Measures S-roots (short, falling pitch, creaky/glottal) vs L-roots (long, level pitch, breathy); 'Other pitch contours in the language were not found to be phonologically distinctive'; favours an underlying final glottal stop analysis with a 'heavy root constraint' (every root closed or long; prefixes exempt).
